title: Headroom experiments: KV burst-absorbing behavior and eviction churn
body:
Overview:

This doc summarizes a set of exploratory runs aimed at quantifying how much short-term headroom our KV cache can absorb during sudden arrival-rate bursts and what eviction/paging side effects happen when we exceed that headroom. Motivation is to understand failure modes for low-latency SLOs under bursty traffic and to tune admission/prefetch/backpressure knobs in Dedicated.

Motivation and goals (short):
- Measure the transient reuse rate deltas during bursts (0–30s, 30–120s, >120s).
- Estimate the "burst-absorbing headroom" in terms of resident pages and memory-bandwidth before NVMe spillback increases token latency by >10ms.
- Identify eviction-churn signatures that correlate with long-tail tail-latency (>99.9th).
- Produce pragmatic mitigations (pin thresholds, delay-prefetch windows, adaptive admission) to prototype in next sprint.

Experiment setup:
- Binary: serving-runtime branch headroom-experiments (hooked instrumentation).
- Hardware: 8x A100(80GB) multi-GPU node configured single tenant to isolate cache interference.
- Cache config baseline: 48GB resident allocation for KV, LRU-ish eviction with per-bank fairness, prefetch enabled (window=6), spillback to NVMe (direct-io).
- Synthetic workload: mixture sampler derived from production trace (sample id: burst-8-2024). Workload shapes: steady (100 qps), burst-short (1.6k qps for 15s), burst-long (800 qps for 90s), mixed seqlen (avg=512, tail=4096).
- Telemetry collected: resident_set_size, per-bank bandwidth (GB/s), eviction_count/s, pages_spilled/s, reuse_rate (per-request prefix match fraction), per-request latency p50/p95/p99/p999, KV lookup CPU samples, VBuf allocations, NVMe IO tail latency.

Instrumentation notes (what we added):
- Lightweight reuse sampler (1/200 sampling) that records last-touch delta per key and whether the lookup hit a resident page. Output: reuse_histogram per-second.
- Eviction trace pipeline: on-evict emit (timestamp, page_id_hash, size, bank_id, last_touch_delta).
- Bandwidth meters per rail (rail = memory channel) and per-bank moving window avg (100ms).
- Burst marker: test harness emits burst_id to logs so we can align traces.

Workload series and runs (id mapping):
- run-A (steady baseline)
- run-B (short burst)
- run-C (long burst)
- run-D (long burst + reduced resident by 20%)
- run-E (long burst + aggressive prefetch off)

Key results (annotated):
- Baseline (run-A): reuse_rate avg=41%, reuse_rate tail (top 5%) ~68%. Resident pages stable; eviction_count < 12/s. Latency p999 = 18.3ms.
- Short burst (run-B): immediate drop in reuse_rate to 22% during burst crest (0–8s), then recovery to ~36% within 40s. Bandwidth per-rail spiked to 82% of measured saturation. Eviction_count peaked 4x baseline; NVMe spillback negligible. Tail latency p999 increased to 31.6ms during crest, then recovered.
- Long burst (run-C): reuse_rate collapsed to 15% for the first 60s, slow recovery — did not return to baseline inside 5-minute observation window when resident set pinned at baseline. Eviction_count sustained at 3x baseline; pages_spilled/s increased and NVMe IO tail moved from 2ms median to 28ms 95th. Latency p999 jumped to 98ms and correlated with NVMe tail events.
- Reduced resident (run-D): when resident set reduced by 20%, the system entered spillback earlier (burst headroom decreased ~28%), p999 hit 140ms and sustained while burst lasted.
- Prefetch off (run-E): turning off speculative prefetch reduced eviction churn by ~22% but increased average lookup CPU time; reuse_rate slightly lower on crest but NVMe spillback events were 40% fewer and overall p999 improved during long bursts.

Observations and interpretable signals:
1) Two regimes: (A) short bursts (~<20s) where bandwidth headroom is primary limiter and recovery is fast; (B) sustained bursts (>30s) where eviction pressure + NVMe spillback cascades into long tail latency.
2) Reuse-rate is the most sensitive early indicator — a sharp drop to <25% within 10s predicts sustained spillback with >90% precision in our runs.
3) Eviction churn pattern: many small evictions (page size aligned) with high last_touch_delta variance -> those correlate with later NVMe spikes. Contrast with fewer, larger evictions which had less latency impact because they were preceded by controlled prefetch drain.
4) Per-rail bandwidth imbalance: when one rail hit >82% while others were <60%, we saw localized bank saturation -> increased stalls and higher eviction_count on that bank. Headroom should be estimated per-rail not just aggregate.
5) Prefetching tradeoff: speculative prefetch helps short bursts by increasing apparent reuse (fills hot windows) but for long bursts it amplifies eviction churn and pushes more cold pages to NVMe.

Hypotheses we want to test next (from observed signals):
- H1: A short-term gate based on reuse-rate drop (sampled) plus per-rail bandwidth threshold can trigger conservative admission (shed or downgrade) and avoid NVMe spillback for 80% of sustained bursts.
- H2: A per-bank pinning guard (protect top-X hot pages per-bank by last_touch_delta threshold) reduces eviction churn and NVMe spill events, trading small resident increase for tail-latency reduction.
- H3: Adaptive prefetch window: increase for short bursts (<20s) and shrink for sustained bursts; switching must be hysteretic to avoid oscillation.

Quick flamegraph / CPU profile notes:
- Hot path during crest: KV lookup mutex contention and memmove from prefetch buffers showed up in top CPU stacks; indicates prefetch and eviction coordination in the CPU path matters.
- A small fraction (<2%) of requests incurred an extra syscall path when NVMe hit, causing context switches that amplified latency spikes.

Concrete numbers to carry forward for SLOs and knobs:
- Burst-absorbing headroom estimate (median): 12–16GB of extra resident allocation above baseline for short bursts to keep p999 < 40ms. For our hardware and workload shape that equates to ~110–160k pages (page_size=128KB equivalent to our internal chunking).
- Per-rail safe bandwidth threshold: target ~72% of measured sustained saturation (give 10% guard). When one rail >82% consider throttling incoming admission.
- Reuse-rate threshold to trigger preemptive action: sampled reuse_rate <= 28% for two consecutive 1s windows -> signal for throttle/downscale.

Immediate recommended mitigations (prototype):
- Implement sampled reuse-rate monitor (low-cost) + per-rail meter and a simple policy: if reuse_rate <= 28% && any rail >80% -> engage conservative admission for 10s.
- Add per-bank hotpage protection: keep top-2 pages per-bank pinned if last_touch_delta < 3s; add telemetry to measure memory overhead and hit improvement.
- Quick A/B: in Dedicated run with aggressive prefetch off policy and pinning enabled compare p999 under long bursts.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How representative is burst-8-2024 sample of multi-tenant Dedicated traffic? Need cross-tenant trace mixes to validate.
- Long-term interaction with auto-scaler: if we throttle application-level admission, auto-scaler may interpret that as low throughput and scale down - need controller-level coordination.
- Prefetch tuning delta by model architecture/seq len distribution — current tests limited to Llama-style model traces.

Next steps / action items:
- (Priya) Ship sampled reuse-rate probe to main branch behind a flag (INF-8461) by next week.
- (Ethan) Implement conservative admission prototype plus per-rail meter (spike detection) and run long-burst A/B in staging (run matrix: with/without pinning, with/without prefetch). Due: 2 weeks.
- (Marta) Collect 5 more production-sampled traces across tenants (different seqlen distributions) and generate workload matrix.
- (Chen) Add a lightweight per-bank pinned-pages telemetry and cost accounting to quantify resident overhead.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is exploratory; numbers are useful as directional guidance not final thresholds.
- Please call out any missing telemetry that would make these signals more actionable (e.g., per-request correlation id propagation between runtime and IO stack).

Appendix: example sampled eviction record (one-line JSON from trace)
{"ts":1709783140.512, "page":"0x7f9b2f3c", "bank":3, "size":131072, "last_touch_delta_ms":74210, "evict_reason":"pressure"}

Quick TODOs (scratch):
- Run the prefetch-off + pinning A/B with different resident sizes (baseline ±10/20%)
- Add per-request flag propagate so we can join KV hits with request latency traces in tracing UI
- Investigate whether moving prefetch to a background worker thread reduces main lookup CPU pressure

End of notes.
